questions.question: Two fair dice are rolled. What is the probability that the sum is 7?
questions.rationale: Six ordered pairs give sum 7 — (1,6), (2,5), (3,4), (4,3), (5,2), (6,1) — out of 36 equally likely pairs: 6/36 = 1/6.

questions.question: Two fair coins are tossed. What is the probability of at least one head?
questions.rationale: The four outcomes are HH, HT, TH, TT; only TT fails the event, so P = 3/4. Equivalently 1 − P(no heads) = 1 − 1/4.

questions.question: One card is drawn from a standard deck. What is P(king or heart)?
questions.rationale: Count carefully: 4 kings + 13 hearts − 1 king of hearts (counted twice) = 16 favourable cards, so P = 16/52 = 4/13. Adding 4 + 13 double-counts.

questions.question: How many face cards are in a standard 52-card deck?
questions.rationale: Each of the 4 suits has 3 face cards (J, Q, K), giving 12 in total; the deck also has 4 aces and 26 red cards.

questions.question: If P(E) = 0.3, what is P(not E)?
questions.rationale: The complement rule gives P(not E) = 1 − P(E) = 1 − 0.3 = 0.7.

questions.question: A fair coin is tossed three times. What is the probability of at least one tail?
questions.rationale: "At least one" wants the complement: 1 − P(all heads) = 1 − 1/8 = 7/8, since only HHH avoids tails.

questions.question: Two events are mutually exclusive. Which statement is TRUE?
questions.rationale: Mutually exclusive events cannot both occur, so P(A and B) = 0 and the addition rule loses its overlap term. Independence is a different concept entirely.

questions.question: Two fair coins are tossed. What is the probability that both show heads?
questions.rationale: The tosses are independent, so P(H and H) = 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4.

questions.question: Two cards are drawn without replacement. What is the probability that both are kings?
questions.rationale: Without replacement the draws are dependent: 4/52 × 3/51 = 12/2652 = 1/221, because one king is already gone.

questions.question: After 200 coin tosses, heads appeared 104 times. Which statement is correct?
options: The coin must be biased, as 104 ≠ 100
This experimental estimate is 0.52 and will settle near 0.5 as trials grow
questions.rationale: Experimental probability is observed frequency (104/200 = 0.52); the law of large numbers says it drifts toward the theoretical 1/2 as the number of trials grows.
